Why quotes vary

      
    
        
  • Gutter length — pros price cleaning and guards largely by the linear foot.
    • 
        
  • Stories & access — a 2- or 3-story home takes longer ladders, more safety gear, more time.
    • 
        
  • Debris load — a gutter full of wet, compacted leaves costs more than a light seasonal clean.
    • 
        
  • Roof pitch & complexity — steep roofs and lots of corners slow the crew down.
    • 
        
  • Season — fall is peak season; booking before the rush (or right after leaf-drop) gets better slots and sometimes better prices.
    • 
        
  • Local labor rates — secondary metros often price below the biggest coastal cities for the same job.
    • 
      

    


    

      
Gutter cleaning vs. gutter guard installation

      
The most common question we see: keep cleaning twice a year, or pay once for guards? The honest math, using the Angi and Dataintelo ranges above:

      

        

          
Keep cleaning

          
    
            
  • $150–$250 per visit, twice a year ≈ $300–$500/yr
    • 
            
  • No upfront cost; works on any gutter
    • 
            
  • Pro spots roof and fascia problems early, every visit
    • 
            
  • You are on the schedule forever — skip a fall and you risk overflow damage
    • 
          

        

        

          
Install guards

          
    
            
  • $6–$13/ft installed — about $1,200–$2,600 for a typical 200 ft home
    • 
            
  • Pays back in roughly 4–8 years versus twice-yearly cleaning on tree-heavy lots
    • 
            
  • Cuts cleaning to an occasional rinse and inspection — it does not eliminate maintenance
    • 
            
  • Best under big leaf-dropping trees; micro-mesh handles pine needles and shingle grit
    • 
          

        

      

      
Rule of thumb: few trees near the roof → keep cleaning. Roof buried in oak, maple, or pine → guards usually win. Either way, guards go onto clean, well-sloped gutters, so a cleaning and any repairs come first.

    


    

      
Fall gutter cleaning checklist

      
October through November is the most important gutter window of the year in the Northeast, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest. Work through this list before the first hard freeze:

      
      
    
        
  • Clear the full run — leaves, twigs, shingle grit, and the mud layer at the bottom of the gutter.
    • 
        
  • Flush every downspout — a clear gutter with a blocked downspout still overflows. Pros rod or flush clogs from the top.
    • 
        
  • Check the slope — water should move to the downspout, not pool. Standing water means a re-pitch ($80–$250).
    • 
        
  • Inspect seams and corners — fall is when small leaks show. Resealing runs $80–$140 now, versus rot repair later.
    • 
        
  • Look at hangers and fascia — sagging sections ($80–$600 to fix) get worse under ice and snow load.
    • 
        
  • Trim back overhanging branches — less debris next season, fewer critters using the roof as a highway.
    • 
        
  • Decide on guards before winter — if you cleaned three times this year, run the guard math in the section above.
    • 
        
  • Book early — in leaf season the best local crews book out one to three weeks. Urgent overflow? Say so in your request — pros triage active water problems first.
    • 
      

    


    

      
How often should gutters be cleaned?

      

        
Minimum: twice a year
Late spring (after seed and blossom drop) and late fall (after leaf drop). This is the baseline for most US homes.

        
Tree-heavy lots: 3–4× a year
Oaks, maples, and pines over the roofline fill gutters fast. The Northeast, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest see the heaviest demand — and most pros there recommend the twice-yearly minimum as a floor, not a target.

        
With guards: 1–2 checks a year
Guards slow the fill; they don't stop it. A spring rinse and fall inspection keep the system honest and the warranty valid.

      

      
Prevention is the trend: 52% of homeowners now invest in preventive home maintenance rather than waiting for damage (Business Research Insights, third-party estimate). A $150–$250 cleaning is the cheapest line item in that plan — foundation and fascia repairs are not.

    


    

      
Choosing a gutter cleaner you can trust

      
Gutter work isn't a licensed trade in most states, which makes your questions the quality filter. Ask every pro these before you book:

      
    
        
  • "Are you insured?" — liability insurance is the baseline. Anyone on a ladder over your property should carry it; ask for the certificate.
    • 
        
  • "What's included?" — a proper cleaning covers the full run, downspout flush, debris removal from your property, and a basic condition report.
    • 
        
  • "Is the price by the job or by the foot?" — either is fine, but get it in writing before work starts, and compare it with the ranges on this page.
    • 
        
  • "Do you check slope, seams, and hangers while you're up there?" — good crews report small problems while they're still $80–$140 problems.
    • 
        
  • "What happens if you find damage?" — you want photos and a written repair quote, not work done first and billed later.
    • 
      

      
Red flags: a quote far above the ranges here with no explanation, pressure to sign today, cash-only with no invoice, or a "free inspection" that turns into a five-figure guard pitch. Verified firms on this site quote the same prices they charge anyone — and because there are no long contracts, they have to earn the job every time.

Frequently asked questions

      
How much does gutter cleaning cost in 2026?
Most homeowners pay $150–$250 for a professional residential cleaning (Dataintelo market data). Angi's 2026 guides put cleaning at $120–$230, and HomeAdvisor lists $105–$190. Two-story homes, long gutter runs, and heavy debris land at the top of the range.

      
How much does gutter repair cost?
Repairs average about $390 and typically run $120–$900 (Angi, 2026). Leak sealing is $80–$140, fixing slope $80–$250, clearing serious clogs $160–$400, physical damage $240–$550, and sagging sections $80–$600.

      
How much do gutter guards cost installed?
$6–$13 per linear foot including materials and labor, with an average project around $1,521 (Angi, 2026). A 200 ft home typically runs $1,200–$2,600. Expect to clean ($120–$230) and repair ($200–$650) the gutters first if they're not in good shape.

      
How often should I clean my gutters?
At least twice a year — late spring and late fall. Homes under heavy tree cover, especially in the Northeast, Midwest, and Pacific Northwest, often need three or four cleanings. With guards installed, plan on one or two inspections a year.

      
Are gutter guards worth it?
On tree-heavy lots, usually: guards at $6–$13/ft pay back in roughly 4–8 years versus $300–$500/year for twice-yearly cleaning. On lots with few trees, regular cleaning is cheaper. Guards reduce cleaning — they never eliminate inspection and the occasional rinse.

      
Why is fall the most important cleaning?
Leaf drop fills gutters in weeks. Wet debris adds weight, overflows onto fascia and foundations, and freezes into ice that can tear runs loose. A fall cleaning before the first hard freeze prevents the most expensive damage.

      
Do quotes from this site cost anything?
No. Building a request pack is free for homeowners, and pros quote the same prices they charge any customer. There are no markups and no obligation to hire anyone who responds.

      
What should a full gutter cleaning include?
Debris removal from the full gutter run, a downspout flush, bagging and removing the debris from your property, and a quick condition check of seams, slope, and hangers — with photos or a written note if the pro finds damage.
